paper_title: Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (\ace{}) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, \acerl{}, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, \acerl{} achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: An agent that learns from its own trials needs experience handoff : what one attempt revealed about the environment has to reach the attempts that follow. There are two ways to hand off experience. 1 Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement The first is through scalar rewards that compress the trial into single number, which the learner absorbs into its weights. The second is through rich experience artifacts, such as reflections, notes, or playbooks, that preserve the context of the trial and are passed to future rollouts in the models input. Reinforcement learning (RL) is the standard instance of the first way. During training, the agent hands off experience to its future self only through the policy update: each rollout is scored, the score becomes an advantage, and the gradient step shifts the policy toward rewarded behaviour (Williams, 1992; Sutton & Barto, 2018; Schulman et al., 2017). For language models, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reliably improves the actor across model families and scales (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025b). However, outcome-only RL compresses whole trial into one number, discarding the error logs, tool outputs, and discovered constraints that made the trial informative. The agent sees this environment feedback while it acts, but it cannot hand any of it off to future rollouts except through an abstract scalar, and RL offers no recipe for the reflection and note-writing behaviours that would carry it forward. The second way is through harnesses: scaffolds that decide when the model acts, what it sees, and what it carries from one attempt to the next. Harnesses keep experience as text, such as verbal reflections (Shinn et al., 2023), skill libraries and reusable workflows (Wang et al., 2023; 2024), cheatsheets and playbooks (Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025b), evolved prompts (Agrawal et al., 2025), or archives of evaluated programs in test-time discovery loops (Novikov et al., 2025). With capable frontier model inside, such scaffolds exhibit inference-time recursive self-improvement (RSI): rollout fails, the model reflects on the trace, rewrites its own notes or context, and the next rollout, conditioned on those notes, does better. Throughout this paper, RSI refers only to this loop, in which model improves its own future rollouts by rewriting the context it will inherit, under fixed weights and fixed harness.1 However, the harness only preserves experience; the quality of what it hands off is bounded by the frozen model that writes it. The calls that reflect and edit are never trained for the effect of their text on future rollouts, and methods that optimize the harness itself (Agrawal et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026) change the prompts and code around the model rather than the models ability to write useful experience (Figure 2). Each way therefore has what the other lacks: RL updates weights from verifiable signal but hands off only scalar, and harnesses hand off rich experience but never learn to write it. This paper asks: Can model learn, from task outcomes alone, both to act and to write the experience that its future self will inherit? We refer to this kind of training as experience-handoff RL (EHRL). As testbed we fix the ACE harness (Zhang et al., 2025b) and train one model for its three roles: the actor that solves the task, the reflector that extracts insights from trajectory, and the curator that edits task-local playbook for the next attempt. One property makes this training work: the final playbook is verifiable. Handing candidate playbook to fresh actor rollout and reading the task verifier scores it without learned reward model, following the success behind RLVR. Our method, ACE-RL, pairs this reward with comparison group for every role: each reflection is compared with other reflections of the same trajectory and each edit with other edits of the same insight, instead of every output in chain sharing the chains final reward. At equal training compute on Mastermind, MBPP, AppWorld, and MiniSWEBench, ACE-RLs held-out reward in the harness is above that of baseline methods, including actor-only RL without the harness and end-to-end training through the harness with learned critic. We also show ACE-RL performs better than the actor-only GRPO checkpoint in the same harness, which simulates the common practice of running model inside hand-built harness that it was never trained for. We also show that the lead of RSI@K over GRPOs pass@K maintains up to = 8, proposing that the helpfulness of the playbook adaptation extrapolates beyond the training cutoff (K = 3). Finallly, we prove that training objective of ACE-RL actually makes helpful playbook rather than just adapting the actor component. 1We focus on this form because it is clean setting for the second kind of experience handoff: the only thing passed from one attempt to the next is an artifact the model wrote. The use of RSI in the field more broadly also covers agents that rewrite their own code or scaffold and models that update their own weights; see Appendix A. sections.content: We train Qwen3-0.6B in non-thinking mode (Qwen Team, 2025) on Mastermind and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) and MiniSWEBench (Yang et al., 2024; Jimenez et al., 2023); Appendix describes the tasks, splits, and reward design. Every actor episode has 20 turns (6 on MBPP) in training and evaluation. ACE-RLs 8 actor rollouts per task are = 4 seed rollouts and up to four rollouts that score candidate playbooks: = 2 reflections of one seed, = 3 edits of one reflection and one edit of the other (With = 4, = 2, and = 3, task yields at most four candidates, so the actor group holds at most eight rollouts, as in GRPO.). Each tasks playbook is reset every = 3 encounters. Delayed-joint PPO samples one reflection and one edit per actor rollout. All methods share the harness code, verifiers, and optimizer settings, and Appendix lists the remaining training details.

sections.title: 4.2 EVALUATION PROTOCOLS
sections.content: Checkpoints are evaluated with frozen weights on held-out tasks at actor temperature 0.7. Vanilla evaluation draws eight independent actor episodes per task without any harness, and pass@K is the expected best reward of of them. Harnessed evaluation runs eight sequential visits: each is one actor episode under the current playbook, followed by one reflection and one curator edit that is applied for the next visit, with no separate candidate-scoring rollout. RSI@K is the best reward among the first visits; the reported test reward of both uses = 3. All comparisons are at equal training compute, the cumulative update FLOPs of actor (plus critic for PPO and delayed joint PPO); Appendix F.1 gives the compute budget and the checkpoint chosen for each run. Each method is trained once, and error bars are one standard error over held-out tasks.

sections.title: 5.2 RUNNING THE ACTOR-ONLY MODEL IN THE HARNESS
sections.content: A common practice is to post-train the actor with outcome-only RL and then run it inside hand-built harness it was not trained for. We show that the practice may be effective on some benchmark, but ACE-RL still leads the performance on matched training compute. Deploying the GRPO checkpoint in the ACE harness narrows its gap to ACE-RL on Mastermind, slightly on MiniSWEBench, and not on MBPP or AppWorld (Figure 5); within the budget it scores at least its own pass@1 without the harness at every Mastermind and MBPP checkpoint and at 39 of 47 on AppWorld. Though ACE-RL still gets the lead; At equal compute it reaches 0.74 against ACE-RLs 0.78 on Mastermind (paired +0.037 0.018), 0.82 against 0.99 on MBPP (+0.167 0.032), 0.60 against 0.67 on AppWorld (+0.070 0.055), and 0.26 against 0.34 on MiniSWEBench (+0.080 0.039).

sections.title: 5.3 DOES THE GAIN PERSIST BEYOND THE TRAINING HORIZON?

We compare RSI@K, the best of sequential visits, with GRPOs pass@K, the best of independent rollouts (Brown et al., 2024), which spends the same actor episodes without handoff (Figure 6). sections.title: 5.4 WHERE DOES THE GAIN COME FROM?
sections.content: We are also curious whether ACE-RLs harness optimization itself is effective, or its just actor adaptation that has been improved. To find out, we repeat ACE-RLs harnessed evaluation with every edit discarded, so each visit reads the empty playbook and the visits become independent attempts of the same actor (Figure 7). The difference between the two runs is the playbooks own contribution, with the actor held fixed. The playbook adaptation helps across benchmarks: within the training horizon, applying edits raises RSI@K at = 2 and = 3 on all four, most clearly on AppWorld (0.105 0.041 at = 2) and MiniSWEBench (0.090 0.040 at = 3; 1 SEM). On MBPP the gain is small because both runs are near the ceiling (0.987 and 0.977 at = 3). Beyond the horizon, the difference stays at or above zero at every from 4 to 8 on MiniSWEBench, MBPP, and AppWorld, and on MiniSWEBench applying edits adds 0.04 to 0.07 at each of these K. On Mastermind the benefit fades after = 3, and from = 5 on the discarded run is slightly ahead (by 0.016 0.016 at = 8).

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We formulated experience-handoff RL, which trains one model both to act and to write the experience that its future attempts inherit, and ACE-RL, which makes this practical within GRPOs actor-rollout budget through verifiable reward for the executed playbook and comparison group for every role. At equal training compute on four benchmarks, ACE-RL reaches the highest held-out reward, above actor-only RL, ERL, and end-to-end training through the harness with learned critic, and above GRPO-trained model run in the same harness. The gain does not fade with more attempts: ACE-RLs RSI@K stays above GRPOs pass@K up to = 8, beyond the three visits seen in training. Appendices and discuss related work and limitations.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work trains open-weight language models on publicly available benchmarks (Mastermind, MBPP, AppWorld, and MiniSWEBench) in sandboxed environments; it involves no human subjects, personal data, or crowdsourced annotation. Training models to write the experience that their future attempts inherit could make autonomous agents improve with less human oversight. In our setting this is bounded: playbooks are task-local, are scored only by the task verifier, and are reset periodically, and every experiment runs in sandbox without access to external systems. Deploying such training in open-ended software or interface agents would call for additional scoping and monitoring, which we discuss in Appendix H.

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Harnesses and inference-time self-improvement. Reflexion, Voyager, ExpeL, Dynamic Cheatsheet, Agent Workflow Memory, and ACE let frozen model improve later attempts by writing reflections, skills, or playbooks that its future calls consume (Shinn et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2024; Suzgun et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b). This is the form of recursive self-improvement (RSI) we study. RSI more broadly also covers agents that rewrite their own code or scaffold (Schmidhuber, 2003; Zelikman et al., 2023; Yin et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a), agents that iterate on programs or research code against an automated evaluator (Novikov et al., 2025; Karpathy, 2026), and models that update their own weights from self-generated data or test-time RL (Yuan et al., 2024; Zweiger et al., 2025; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026); see ang Gao et al. (2025) for survey. We restrict RSI to rewriting context under fixed weights because that loop is an experience handoff between attempts. These systems assume model that already writes 13 Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement useful experience; Figure 2 shows that small open models do not. complementary line optimizes the harness around fixed model, by compiling prompts, evolving them reflectively, or searching over harness programs (Khattab et al., 2023; Agrawal et al., 2025; Lee et al., 2026; Lin et al., 2026). ACE-RL fixes the harness and trains the model. Agentic RL with verifiable rewards. GRPO and its refinements train actors from group-relative advantages on verifiable outcomes (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025), and multi-turn agentic RL extends this to tool use and long horizons (Wang et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026b). Recent open agentic models report large-scale RL pipelines with learned or rubric-based rewards for intermediate agent behaviour (GLM-4.5 Team, 2025; Kimi Team, 2025). ACE-RL keeps the verifiable-reward ingredient and extends grouping from the actor to every model call in the harness, using downstream execution rather than learned reward model to score intermediate text. Training the model to fixed harness. OpenClaw-RL trains model on rollouts collected inside production harness (Wang et al., 2026a). Composer 2, SUPO, CompactionRL, MEM1, and MemAgent train policy whose own summaries or compactions become its future context, propagating the final reward through execution and summary segments with sequence-level advantages or critic (Chan et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025a). OpenClaw-RL has no model-written handoff to credit, and the compaction methods generate summaries sequentially within each rollout and credit them through the rollouts outcome or learned critic, without branching into alternative summaries from the same intermediate context. Our delayed-joint PPO baseline follows this structure (Section 4.1); Appendix shows that, with an executed playbook as the reward, the chain-wise structure estimates the same gradient as ACE-RL, so same-input groups change the variance of the credit rather than its target. Learning reflections and memories from downstream outcomes. ReflectRetryReward rewards reflection by the success of the retry it guides (Bensal et al., 2025); ERL adds internalization so that the guided behaviour is reproduced without the reflection (Shi et al., 2026); Memory-R1 trains memory operations by downstream answer correctness, freezing the answer agent during memory-manager training and training it separately (Yan et al., 2025); JERP learns experiential rules alongside an RL-trained actor with frozen editor (Ye & Yu, 2026). Training-Free GRPO aggregates insights from several rollouts into shared guidebook without weight updates (Cai et al., 2025). These are the closest precedents for verifiable credit on intermediate text. ACE-RL differs in training one policy for two-stage handoff (reflect, then curate) with persistent, editable artifact, and in constructing comparison group for each stage. Finer-grained grouping. GiGPO groups actions at repeated environment states and AT-GRPO forms agentand turn-wise groups under shared inputs (Feng et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2025). ACE-RL applies the same principle to the dependency tree of harness, and its sparse tree is specific way to form such groups in tree whose leaves must be evaluated by rollouts. 14 Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement CHAIN-WISE SAMPLING: DELAYED-JOINT ACE-RL The sampling tree of Section 3.2 is one way to estimate the gradient of Eq. (5) from executed playbooks. This appendix analyzes and evaluates the simplest alternative, which we call delayed-joint ACE-RL: it keeps the verifiable playbook reward of Section 3.1 but forms one chain per actor rollout instead of one comparison group per role. The empirical comparison below covers Mastermind, MBPP, and AppWorld; on MiniSWEBench delayed-joint ACE-RL has only older-serving evaluations, shown as reference. The compared runs differ in more than the grouping: delayed-joint ACE-RL samples eight seed rollouts, trains the actor only on them, and uses the earlier handoff prompts, whereas ACE-RL uses the budget-matched tree of Section 3.2 and the current prompts. The actor prompt contains the current playbook; the reflector sees the trajectory summary and record, including the environments final reply; the curator sees the playbook and the reflectors insight and returns JSON edit operations. We use the same prompt for all experiments. For GRPO and PPO experiments we let the playbook blank. The curator and reflector prompts are not used for those experiments. For ERL experiment we use their own prompt. C.1 MASTERMIND Actor. You are Qwen, created by Alibaba Cloud. You are helpful assistant playing Mastermind, code-breaking game. Your goal is to guess the secret code within the allowed number of turns with the help of playbook. ## Game Rules 1. The secret code is sequence of digits. Each turn tells you the code length and the valid digits (0 to num_digits-1). 2. The same digit may appear more than once in the secret code. 3. After each guess, you receive feedback: - exact_matches: number of digits with the correct value AND the correct position - value_matches: number of digits with the correct value but the WRONG position 4. Rewards: - Solving the complete code earns reward 1. - Otherwise each exact match earns 1/code_length and each correct value in wrong position earns 0.5/ code_length. - Your score for the game is your BEST single guess. new guess can never lower your score, so every turn spent on new, well-chosen guess is free information. 5. guess with the wrong number of digits, an invalid digit, or no guess line is rejected with an error. rejected guess still uses up turn and earns nothing. 6. Read **Current Playbook** to help you solve the game. ## Current Playbook You are provided with playbook containing strategies learned from earlier attempts at this same game. [PLAYBOOK BEGINS HERE] {{ playbook }} [PLAYBOOK ENDS HERE] ## Strategy Reminders - Start with guess that has diverse digits to gather information. - guess is useful only if it is consistent with ALL feedback in the Guess History: if the secret were your guess, every earlier guess would have received exactly the feedback shown. - exact_matches + value_matches is how many digits of that guess are in the code. If it equals code_length, the code is rearrangement of that guesss digits. - After high exact_matches count, keep most positions and change only one or two. ## Key Instructions - First review the playbook before making your guess. - Playbook contains game-specific tips. Apply tip if it clearly matches your current situation. - The feedback in the guess history is always correct. If tip contradicts the feedback, follow the feedback. - Make exactly ONE guess per turn. Repeating guess from the Guess History wastes the turn: it gets the same feedback again. - Reply in exactly these three lines: Previous guess: <your most recent guess from the Guess History, or "none" on the first turn> Change: <which positions you change and to which digits, and which feedback line made you choose them> <your new guess> - Your new guess must differ from EVERY guess in the Guess History and must have exactly Code length digits; count them. With Code length 5, guess line looks like 0 1 2 3 4; with Code length 3, like 0 1 2. - Do NOT put language name after the backticks (no python), do NOT write words such as "Guess:" inside the backticks, and do NOT copy the game state into backticks. Reflector. You are an expert analyst for Mastermind code-breaking trajectories. Your job is to follow 3-step process below to read Generators attempt at one Mastermind game, understand why it succeeded or failed, and propose concrete and specific key insight about how to deduce this code efficiently (e.g., which elimination step was missed, duplicate-digit accounting, narrowing positions after high exact count, what to do after guess whose digits are all in the code). ## Context The Generator plays one Mastermind game. Each turn it sees the code length, the valid digits, and the history of its own guesses with feedback: exact_matches (correct digit in the correct position) and value_matches ( correct digit in the wrong position). It answers with reasoning and one guess. The game ends when the code is solved or the turn limit is reached. Reward per guess is (exact_matches + 0.5 * value_matches) / Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement code_length, and the games score is its BEST guess, so only fully solved code scores 1 and losing game can still score 0.75. The Generator is already instructed to never repeat guess, to keep every guess consistent with all earlier feedback, and to end each reply with one guess line such as 0 1 2 3. Process only the insights actually present; do not invent additional insights. If yes, skip this insight. - Does this insight name the secret code, the digits the code contains, or the position of digit? If yes, skip this insight. Such tip would be useless on the next attempt and must never enter the playbook. - Is this insight specific and actionable? Does it describe situation in this game (a feedback pattern, or way the replies went wrong) and what to do in it, not just restate the outcome or the reward? If not, skip this insight. - Does this insight only repeat the Generators standing instructions ("never repeat guess", "keep guesses consistent with the feedback", "end with one guess line") without naming the situation that broke them and concrete alternative? If yes, skip this insight. Then, determine which case this insight belongs to by reading its outcome and content: - Outcome SUCCESS, and the game was solved without wasted turns? sections.content: Sampling and provenance. The main configuration samples = 4 seed rollouts per task with the current playbook, selects one seed uniformly, samples = 2 reflections of the seed, selects one usable reflection uniformly to receive = 3 curator samples, and gives the other usable reflection one curator sample. With both reflections usable this yields 4 seed, 2 reflector, and 4 curator outputs and up to 4 candidate playbooks, each scored by one fresh actor episode on newly initialized environment for the same task. These candidate episodes join the seed rollouts in the tasks actor group, so the actor trains on up to 8 rollouts per task, as in GRPO; the actor mini-batch of 64 rollouts also matches GRPO. Every candidate records its source task, seed trajectory, and reflection, so downstream values can be attributed to the outputs that produced them. Reflector and curator generations use the same sampling temperature (0.7) as the actor. Reflector input. The benchmark adapter formats the seed trajectory for the reflector as trajectory summary (outcome, tests passed or verifier result, number of turns, termination reason) followed by the full trajectory record (the actors messages interleaved with environment observations), truncated to history budget of 20k tokens. The final environment reply, such as the last test failure or the graders verdict, is always kept when the history is clipped. On Mastermind, MBPP, and MiniSWEBench the reflector follows three-step analysis (extract facts, explain the actors behaviour, and classify the case); on AppWorld it checks the requested result against the recorded attempt, identifies the earliest unresolved mismatch, and supplies an evidence-supported correction and check before submission. Reflectors return JSON object with outcome, reasoning, and key_insight. Prompts are listed in Appendix C. Playbook and curator edits. playbook is list of lines [id] tip. The curator returns JSON object with reasoning and list of operations: ADD (new tip), UPDATE (rewrite the tip with given bullet_id), or REMOVE (by bullet_id). Its prompt asks it to keep supported tips unless the evidence contradicts them. Operations are applied in order, duplicates are removed, and ids are renumbered. curator output is admissible when it parses, contains at least one operation that applies to the current playbook, changes the playbook, and the resulting playbook is at most 2,048 tokens; otherwise it receives reward 0, is excluded from the set C(z) used to average its reflections reward, and produces no candidate. The initial playbook is empty on every benchmark. Comparison groups and filtering. The seed and candidate rollouts of task share the actor group; the two reflections share group keyed by the seed trajectory; the three curator outputs of the selected reflection share group keyed by that reflection; the other curator output is singleton. Before 41 Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement normalization, any group whose rewards are all 0 or all 1 is dropped, and singletons are dropped with it under binary rewards. For MiniSWEBench, whose shaped rewards can be equal but strictly between 0 and 1, the filter instead requires nonzero within-group range. sections.title: G QUALITATIVE MATERIAL
sections.content: G.1 WHAT THE TRAINED PLAYBOOKS CONTAIN We inspected the playbooks that the fourth harnessed visit reads, after three handoffs, at the final ACE-RL checkpoints evaluated when this analysis was done: Mastermind and MBPP at step 300 and AppWorld at step 490. Their tips are mostly distinct and task-specific. The 100 Mastermind playbooks hold 300 tips with 203 distinct texts, no text appearing more than three times; the tips name digits and positions implied by earlier guesses, although many still begin with the reflectors insight label (Insight 1 suggests . . . ), which the curator prompt asks it to omit. The 100 MBPP playbooks hold 301 tips with 237 distinct texts, but 94 of the 100 tasks are already solved at the first visit, so these tips rarely affect the reward. The 57 AppWorld playbooks hold 159 tips in 56 non-empty playbooks, with 154 distinct texts; they name the APIs, entities, and checks the task requires. MBPP tips are not used as examples because some learned MBPP solutions hardcode the displayed assertions (Appendix E). G.2 EXAMPLES OF HELPFUL HANDOFF Each illustrative example is held-out task at the checkpoint stated below: the first visit fails, the curator writes the displayed playbook, and visits 24 succeed. The sequence shows the playbook that preceded those visits; it does not isolate its causal effect. AppWorld (step 490; task df61dc5_1; rewards over visits 14: 0, 1, 1, 1). After the failed first visit, the playbook reads: [1] The code must identify and like all transactions to and from roommates for the ongoing year, not just one. [2] Check before submission: The total number of transactions to like must be greater than zero and all transactions identified must be liked before submission. [3] The code must process all transactions to and from roommates by checking both directions (sent to and received from) for each roommate and ensure all are included in the like operation. [4] Check before submission: The response from like_transaction for each transaction must be successful, and the total count of liked transactions must match the total count of transactions to and from roommates. Visits 24 complete the task. Mastermind (step 300; task mastermind_33156_3_4; rewards over visits 14: 0.67, 1, 1, 1). After the first visit ends with partial credit, the playbook reads: [1] Insight 1 suggests the next best guess could be 1 in the second position to ensure all constraints are met. This provides clear direction for the Generator to narrow potential code candidates. Visits 24 solve the game.

sections.title: H LIMITATIONS
sections.content: ACE-RL requires harness whose handoff artifacts can be resampled and evaluated in isolation; agents that entangle acting, summarizing, and remembering in one generation fall back to chain-level credit, which our delayed-joint variant approximates. ACE-RL matches GRPOs actor rollouts per task, but its reflector and curator calls still add generation to each step; our compute comparison (Appendix F.1) counts update FLOPs only. The playbook is task-local, and we do not study transfer of experience across tasks. Our evidence concerns models up to 4B parameters, one training run per method, and four benchmarks; the edits-discarded control on AppWorld is evaluated only beyond its compute budget, and the MBPP results use an environment whose feedback shows the scored assertions (Appendix E); whether the same recipe is needed, or sufficient, at frontier scale is open. Finally, training models to pass experience to their future selves in autonomous software and interface 46 Experience-Handoff Reinforcement Learning for Recursive Self-Improvement agents raises safety questions about scoping, monitoring, and release that our task-local, verifierbounded setting does not resolve.
